tier_reason: First-party LD_PRELOAD runs of scalloc-artifact benchmarks (threadtest, shbench, rpmalloc-benchmark producer-consumer) against ptmalloc2 (glibc 2.19), a 2017 jemalloc dev build, llalloc and rpmalloc on dual Xeon E5-2620v4 under WSL; results only as plots normalised to ptmalloc2, no compiler or flags, and the modified harness is not in the repo, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Qualitative from plots normalised to ptmalloc2 (no ratios in text): highest throughput on threadtest small objects except at 32 threads where it is a bit behind jemalloc; top on threadtest medium objects at 32 threads; on shbench out-performs all competitors in throughput and memory at higher core counts but lags llalloc at low thread counts; highest throughput on producer-consumer at the cost of more memory. ptmalloc2 is described as consistently the slowest.
corrections.baseline: glibc ptmalloc2 (glibc 2.19) and jemalloc (dev build, August 2017); also llalloc and rpmalloc
corrections.workload: threadtest and shbench (small <=64 B and medium few-KB objects) from the scalloc artifact, plus rpmalloc-benchmark in producer-consumer mode, at 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 and 32 threads via LD_PRELOAD.
corrections.caveats: First-party results run on WSL, compiler flags not stated, results are plot-only (no numeric ratios); harness is a locally modified scalloc-artifact not checked into the repo; old baselines (glibc 2.19 ptmalloc2, 2017 jemalloc dev); higher memory use than competitors on threadtest and producer-consumer; page is marked work in progress; unmaintained since 2020; mimalloc not compared.

tier_reason: Public harness (benchmarks/benchsuite/bench_compare.py, bench_suite) with GCC 14.2 -O3 -march=native + LTO stated in docs/performance_report.md, but the hardware is only '2 vCPU x86-64 VM (Intel Xeon)' with no CPU model, so it falls short of A; first-party, so C.

corrections.hardware: 2-vCPU x86-64 VM (Intel Xeon, model not stated), 4 GB RAM, Debian 13; T=4 is 2x oversubscribed; glibc 2.41
corrections.claimed_speedup: Wins 20/33 throughput cells vs glibc, 21/33 vs jemalloc, 12/33 vs mimalloc. Vs glibc: small-mixed 1.24-1.51x, random 1-4096 B up to 2.98x, ramp 1.54-1.94x. Large-block cycles 6.8-14.6x faster than jemalloc and 4.6-9.2x faster than mimalloc. Retains 16.0 MB vs 46.7/171.8/552.2 MB (glibc/jemalloc/mimalloc) after purging 1M objects. Loses on realloc-grow (0.28x vs glibc), thread-churn vs glibc (0.48-0.62x), bulk 1M alloc+free (0.63-0.77x vs glibc), churn vs jemalloc/mimalloc (0.55-0.75x) and ramp vs mimalloc (0.36-0.51x).
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers on a 2-vCPU VM with CPU model missing, T=4 oversubscribed; the report itself warns contended cells are noisy and to quote the win/loss pattern, not individual multipliers. Does not beat mimalloc overall (12/33 cells). Raw results are gitignored, so only the summary report is public. Very new repo (3 stars, last commit 'Restore repository to a2a342b6 baseline' on 2026-10-02). In-process gbench ratios up to 50-285x are page-fault artifacts per the author.

notes: MIT LICENSE file confirmed. Numbers checked in docs/performance_report.md and README; they match the record apart from the large-block range split (jemalloc 6.8-14.6x, mimalloc 4.6-9.2x).
